variants.text: She's the Godspeed Ginny. Somebody named her that. Four knots. Downhill. With a tailwind.
Godspeed Ginny. The name was optimistic and the boat has never once agreed with it.
Yes, Godspeed. No, I don't know who. Whoever it was never met her.
That BREEZY showing through the transom? Previous owner. Lovely woman. Terrible sailor.
You've spotted BREEZY under the paint. That was a horse. Long story. Don't ask the horse.
BREEZY? That's not a name, that's a warning about the starboard rail.
Ahead of you — KNIGHT FALLS. Forty-two cubits of thundering water. Forty-two. Cubits.
Forty-two cubits, folks. I'm required to say it. I've never been told what a cubit is.
Forty-two cubits. That's the figure in the brochure and I stand behind the brochure.
variants.follow: Water comes over the rail and over everyone's head and, yes, behind the brochure.

variants.text: Named for a knight who went over it in armour. Or a surveyor named Knight. Or it's just 'night,' spelled wrong. Pick one.
Knight Falls. Named after Sir somebody. The chart's the only record and the chart is a rumour.
No. Don't jump. NOT THAT KIND OF BAIL.
THE BUCKET. SIR. The bucket. Sit down.
I said bail. I meant the buckets. We have been over this.
Two ducks, one either side. Steer between them and you create a para-ducks.
Duck to port, duck to starboard. Straight up the middle and we've got ourselves a para-ducks.
Duck… duck… GOOSE.
Two ducks and a— that's a goose. That's a goose, folks.
Duck. Duck. …I had something for this.
I had shares in that mine. Of all the things I've lost in my life, it's my mine I miss the most.
Shares. In that. Bought high. I lost my mine, and I think about it most days.
I worked for White Star Line. …We'll leave it there.
Before this? White Star Line. I'd rather not go into it.
White Star. Yes. That White Star. No further questions.
I served on the poop deck. …It's a real term. It's from the French. La poupe. It's in the— stop laughing. That job stunk.
Poop deck. Raised deck aft. Nautical term, centuries old. And yes. That job stunk.
My first posting was the poop deck. I'd thank you not to make it a thing. It was already a thing. It stunk.
Off the port bow — the Calliope. Aground since '33. Same chart, same fork, same wide water and good bottom. That, folks, is a steaming pile.
She was the pride of the upper river. Now she's a steaming pile. And I do mean steaming. Boiler's still going. Nobody's told it.
That's the competition. Sorry — that WAS the competition. Steam launch, hard aground, listing. A steaming pile.

title: He read the same three words

variants.text: Same chart as mine. Same fork. He read the same three words I read. I just read them slower.
There's no version of this where I'm better than him. There's only a version where I was slower that day.
Reverse is more of a suggestion on this boat. So whatever's ahead — we're going in.
She doesn't back up. She's never backed up. We commit, or we discuss it with the bank.
Safety valve's painted shut. Pressure only goes one way. Good news — the fix is more speed.
When she starts screaming, we go faster. I know. I've stopped arguing with it.
Chart calls this stretch wide water, good bottom. Named after someone the surveyor met that season. …I hear it. I hear it now.
'Wide water, good bottom,' it says. In his handwriting. Named for a personal acquaintance. I'm going to keep going.
Hippopotamus. Four tons, opens to a hundred and fifty degrees. That's not a yawn, that's an appointment.
They look sleepy. They are not sleepy. They are the least sleepy animal on this river.
The chart says crocodile. I have looked. I am still looking. If you see one, do not tell me — I have a bit.
Crocodile Bend. Named in hope. Stocked in never. I apologise on behalf of the reptiles.
Home port's Cra-Zi. Spelled on the chart the way a drunk surveyor heard it. Everyone here says Crazy. Everyone here is wrong.
Cra-Zi. Two syllables, one hyphen, zero relation to what the locals actually call it.
That sign says NOWHERE — THREE DAYS. It said that yesterday. It'll say it tomorrow. From either direction.
You want to go to Nowhere? Everyone does. It's three days. It's always three days.
The crate? Cargo. Nothing to— the telegram said LEOPARD SPOTTED. Then SPOTTED LEOPARD. I never got a clarification.
Don't put fingers through the slats. That's not a rule, that's a eulogy.
That's the piano. It does that every wake. It's been doing it for nine miles. It's in the key of wet.
Yes, the freight is playing. No, I can't stop it. It's a piano with opinions.
Whoever's sitting on the ice — that's mission property and it's melting on your account.
The ice is for the hospital. It is not a bench. Ma'am. It is not a bench.
The river's called the Unnamed. That's not me being coy. He left the box blank and the printer set it in capitals.
You're on the Unnamed River. Named, in the end, by a man who couldn't be bothered to ask.
The Unnamed. Yes. I know. No, there isn't another one.
This water's been called the Unnamed, Sin Nombre, Rio Sem Nome, Sans Nom, and Innominata. Five languages. One word. Nobody asked.
Every outfit that came through wrote down 'unnamed' and thought they were copying the last lot. Four hundred years of that.
Innominata's on the oldest sheet, so that's the one the lawyers use. It means the same as all the others. It means nobody asked.
Some charts say Nonesuch. That's a clerk who read 'no such name' and thought it was pretty.
The Nonesuch. Sounds grand. It's a filing error with good handwriting.
The people who live here have always had a name for it. It's never been on a chart. I'm not going to be the first to spell it wrong.
There is a name. It's a good one. It's just never been official, which is a different thing from never being true.
They could fix the chart. That'd mean a second survey. Nobody's paying for a second survey while the first one still floats most boats.
Every wrong name on this water could be corrected tomorrow. It would cost money. So it won't be.
Every boat on this river runs the same chart. One survey. One season. One man with a flask and a bad ear.
This chart's wrong in the same places for everybody. Comforting, in a way.
I'm not, strictly speaking, licensed. I mention it early so it isn't a surprise later.
Licensing is a complicated subject on this river and I'd rather we enjoyed the trees.
DUCK! …the branch. THE BRANCH. Not the birds. Why are you looking at the birds.
Everybody DUCK — no, down. DOWN. Sir, there are no ducks here.
The river splits around a boulder here. I am conflicted on which way to go. Left or right.
Big rock, two channels. I am conflicted. You are looking at me like that is not a nautical term.
Safety briefing: the boat floats. That's the whole briefing. Please hold us to it.
Rule one: stay in the boat. Rule two: see rule one. There is no rule three; the river keeps eating the paperwork.
Tips are welcome. Refunds are handled by a clerk in Cra-Zi named Dennis, whom I've never met and suspect is a ledger.
Gratuities are optional. Complaints are mandatory, and Dennis reads every one. Dennis is a drawer.
Everything on this cruise is complimentary. That includes the leaks.
Complimentary water is available throughout. Throughout the boat. Mind your shoes.
The brochure said 'leisurely.' It didn't say whose.
The brochure promised 'an unhurried voyage.' Nobody consulted the boiler.
This hat came with the boat. So did the opinions about it.
I've worn this hat for eleven years. It's the only thing aboard that's never let me down, and that is not a compliment to the hat.
One blast on the whistle means hello. Two means brace. Three means I've said something I regret.
The whistle has three settings: polite, urgent, and apology.
Wave to the bank, folks. Nobody's waved at it all week. It'll tell its friends.
Go on, wave. The bank is very shy. It's been that way since the bridge.
First day on the river, I made a rule: never look surprised. I haven't looked surprised since. I've been very, very surprised.
I've never once been surprised on this river. I've only been caught holding the same expression.
I'm told I can't say the boat is 'on her last legs.' She hasn't got legs. It's a technical matter.
People say she's showing her age. She's showing her rivets, which is the same thing with more draught.
The compass points north. The river does not. We've agreed to differ.
Compass says north. River says 'we'll see.' I tend to side with the river; it's bigger.
Photographs are welcome. Flash is discouraged. The river is very sensitive about its chart.
No flash, please. Last time, the river saw how it looked and sulked for a week.
Let's have a moment of silence for the previous skipper. …There. He'd have hated that. He loved noise.
A moment's silence for the last skipper, who retired in a hurry. …Thank you. He sends his regards.
Please remain seated. I can't stop you standing. I can only stop the boat from agreeing with you.
Remain seated, please. The boat is happier, and so, in a small way, am I.
This is the kind of trip you'll tell your grandchildren about. Not because it was good. Because they'll ask where your shoes went.
In five years you'll say, 'That was the day the boat leaked and nobody sued.' I'd like that on a plaque.
I hold a master's licence. I've never been told which subject.
My credentials hang on the wall of my office in Cra-Zi. The wall is in the river. It's a long swim.
If you're under ten, you're in charge of the horizon. Tell me if it moves.
Junior crew, I have a job for you: watch for trouble. If you see any, point at it and say nothing. It's what I do.
Cra-Zi Landing, population forty, if you count the ones on the boat.
The sign says 'Welcome to Cra-Zi.' It's been apologising for itself since 1911.
That pier has held up a hundred years on spite and varnish.
The pier is very proud. It's survived two floods and one town council.
The clock on the landing has been right twice. Both times by accident.
The Cra-Zi clock is always on time for something. We just don't know what.
Wave goodbye to Cra-Zi. It's your last chance. Though it's never waved back, so don't take it personally.
You'll grow to love Cra-Zi. Most people do, from a distance, in about an hour.
She isn't leaking. She's sharing.
The boat isn't taking on water. She's making friends with the river.
Who was Ginny? Nobody asks. Everybody wonders. It's the one mystery on this river I'm paid to keep.
Ginny. Lovely name. Nobody's told me who she was, and I've learned not to push.
She's got two horsepower. Both of them are asleep.
Two horsepower, and neither horse has been consulted.
The anchor is a decorative feature. The last time we used it, it found the river bottom and stayed.
We carry an anchor for morale. Morale's been at the bottom ever since.
Life belts are under the seats. Mostly. One of them is a hat.
Life belts are located under your seat. Please do not wear the one marked 'seat.'
We carry a full crew: one skipper, one boiler, and a boy who left in March.
Crew complement is me. The rest are rumours.
That steam isn't trouble. That's the engine thinking. Don't interrupt it.
She's just letting off steam. We've all been there. I've been there since Tuesday.
That whistle isn't a warning. That's applause. The boiler likes your questions.
She's venting because she's happy. It's the only way she knows how to cheer.
Pressure's normal. It's just that normal for this boiler is closer to 'imminent.'
The gauge says high. The gauge has said high since '09. We've learned to take it as personality.
She's lost faith in me. I can tell by the hissing.
The boiler and I have an understanding. She hisses; I pretend not to notice.
We prefer to call it a 'dynamic water feature.'
The deck is wet by design. We call it a splash zone. The zone is the whole boat.
If your feet are wet, that's the river's way of shaking hands.
Don't worry about the damp. It's just the river checking you're all aboard.
Forecast: scattered showers, concentrated mostly in the boat.
Weather today: fair outside, wet inside. It's rare for both to be accurate.
That creak is structural. The boat is telling us a story. It's a long one, and it ends abruptly.
Listen. That's the hull. She's been through a lot, and she'd like to share.
She isn't damaged. She has character. Character is just damage with a better reputation.
She's not broken. She's seasoned.
We patched it with a postcard from Cra-Zi. It's holding. It says 'Wish you were here.'
That patch is a postcard. It says 'Greetings from Cra-Zi.' I can't promise the greeting is mutual.
The river is four hundred miles long, give or take a bend. Most of the bends are take.
Four hundred miles of river. Four hundred and one, if you count the bit where we turned around.
Current's three knots. Which way, nobody's said. We assume downstream, out of politeness.
The current's gentle today. It's got somewhere to be and it's being polite about it.
That water's brown on purpose. It's keeping its options open.
People ask why the river is that colour. It's embarrassed. It's the colour of everything that's ever fallen in.
There are fish down there. Opinions differ on whether they're ours.
Every fish in this river has a name. None of them answers to it.
That's mist. It's the river's way of saying 'I'm not here.'
The mist rises every morning because the river has learned to hide its mistakes.
The chart was drawn by one man in one afternoon. He was very sure. It's the best thing about him.
The cartographer drew this in a single sitting. We all sat down afterwards, too, out of respect.
The chart marks an X for treasure. I've been to the X. It's a stump. The stump and I have an understanding.
X marks the spot. The spot is a stump. The stump has seen things and doesn't care to discuss them.
The chart has a legend. It says 'Trust me.'
There's a legend in the corner of the chart. It's a single word, and the word is 'probably.'
Scale: one inch to one mile, says the chart. The inch has other ideas.
The chart says one inch equals a mile. I'd measure it, but the ruler has opinions too.
That blank patch says 'here be monsters.' We went. It's mostly mud.
The blank bit on the chart is unexplored, largely because there's nothing there. We checked.
They look sleepy. That's how they get you. Same as the schedule.
Hippos are sleepy, placid and wildly dangerous. You'll find the same in any committee.
That one's yawning. In hippo, that means 'I haven't decided.' In English, it means the same.
That's a lot of mouth. Nobody's asked what's behind it, and I'd advise against it.
They aren't hostile. They're just large and unconcerned about your plans.
Hippos aren't malicious. They simply haven't heard about you and see no reason to start.
We name them. They don't come when called. Neither do I, in fairness.
This is Margaret. That's Dennis. Dennis is the one looking at you.
Tight squeeze. If you've eaten, hold your breath. If you haven't, hold the boat.
It's a squeeze. Please keep your elbows in and your opinions to yourself.
The cut has a marvellous echo. Go on. Say something kind to the river.
Listen to that echo. It's the only thing on the river that agrees with me.
Those walls are covered in the names of skippers who stood right here. Most of them in the past tense.
Carved in the rock: the name of everyone who's come through here. It's a long list. It's still on page one.
That's the Calliope. Aground since '33. She's very comfortable. Please don't wake her.
She hasn't moved in decades. I envy her. She's the only one on this river with a settled schedule.
Good neighbours, the Calliope. Never complains, never moves, never comes to dinner.
The Calliope and I go way back. Mostly she goes back; I go past.
They say she's haunted. The ghost is very polite. It just keeps asking where the exit is.
Locals say she's haunted by the first skipper. He isn't angry. He just doesn't know the way out either.
The only thing coming out of that mine these days is the occasional sigh.
Closed years ago. They found everything in it. Then it ran out of everything.
They used to send a canary in first. These days it's a passenger. Don't worry. I'm joking. Mostly. Sit still.
Old miners sent a canary ahead. I've considered the same system with passengers. Sit still; I'm only considering.
A dead end. It's the nicest way I've found to describe my career.
Dead end. It has a certain charm, if you like a cul-de-sac with a hole in it.
The Reach. So wide you can't see the far bank. We've decided it doesn't exist.
Wide water! Look at all that room. No walls, no rocks, no excuses.
Enjoy the calm. It's the calm they warn you about.
Smooth water. I'm told it's soothing. I find it suspicious.
The river has put up a fence. Nobody asked why. If we did, it would just say 'reasons.'
That's a snag field. It's the river's way of saying 'private.'
Ancient, hollow and utterly uninterested in your opinion of it. That's the timber, not the skipper. Though now you mention it.
These trees fell in a flood nobody wrote down. They haven't forgiven the river, and they've told it so.
If you're wearing a hat, you may want to hold it. If you're not, you may want a hat.
Branches ahead. If you've got a hat, keep it on. If you've got a head, I'd keep that on too.
The crocodiles are on holiday. They sent a postcard. It says 'Wish you weren't here.'
No crocodiles today. They've taken a long weekend. It's the only time anyone on this river gets one.
You can read a crocodile's mood by its teeth. Today, the teeth are elsewhere.
This is where the teeth live. They're away. They'll be back, and they'll want to hear all about it.
The mill's gone. The race stayed. It says it's loyal.
They tore the mill down in '04. The water didn't get the memo. It's still working overtime.
The wheel is long gone. The river keeps turning out of habit. I know the feeling.
A century of grinding corn, and the river still thinks it's got a quota.
It's tradition to leave an offering. Mine is an apology. It's been a long season.
Folks leave flowers. I leave a short note: 'Sorry about earlier.' It's a very general note.
The shrine is to the patron saint of misplaced things. We've lost the paperwork.
Patron of the mislaid. He's very good. Whenever anything goes missing here, it turns up in a surprising place: usually here.
Take a photograph. Whatever's inside will be delighted to be remembered, even as a smudge.
Go on, pose for a snap. If it comes out blurry, that's the saint's way of saying thank you.
Knight Falls. Named for a knight who went over. We don't say which way.
Named for Sir Reginald Knight, who was told 'don't' and was therefore never seen again.
That's genuine falls spray. Or something I did earlier to the boiler. You can't tell, but it feels the same.
Feel that mist? That's a real waterfall. Please don't tell the boiler.
Advertised as mighty. It's a very good water feature. It's a mighty good water feature.
Nine feet of mighty. Which, in a boat, feels like quite a lot more.
Some people go a lifetime without falling nine feet. Today, you're doing it from the comfort of a boat.
Nine feet! That's a long way down, if you've got the right attitude.
Two in front, one behind. That's formation flying. Or a very small queue.
Look at them go. Not a bird among them knows where we're going, and yet they're ahead of us.
That's a goose. Ask it yourself. It'll give you an answer. At length.
The goose has opinions on the river, the boat and you. I'd leave it be.
Left or right. Both are wrong. One is less wrong, and I won't say which.
Left or right? I've done both. I'm told it's good to be consistent, so I've done both.
That boulder has been splitting the river since before there was a river. It's very proud of its work.
The boulder doesn't move. The river does the moving. They've been a team for a thousand years, and it's still unclear who's in charge.
Nowhere is lovely this time of year. It's lovely every time of year. It's the one consistent thing about it.
The weather in Nowhere is always fine, because nobody has stayed long enough to complain.
There's a sign: 'Welcome to Nowhere.' Underneath it is another sign: 'Welcome Back.'
They built a monument to Nowhere. It's very modest. You'll walk past it and not notice. That's the point.
Home is where the boat is. Nowhere is where she ends up.
Everybody who comes to Nowhere is on their way somewhere else. It's the town's one civic virtue.
He's out of tune. The piano, I mean. The man in the boat is fine.
That's a very fine upright. The note you just heard is how it says hello to the river.
The ice is doing its best. The sun is doing its best. Neither is on our side.
It's a block of ice with ambitions. They're mostly in the form of puddles.
The leopard isn't scary. He's misunderstood. And bigger than the sign.
He's a very calm cat. He's also a very large cat. I'd treat those as separate facts.
Mail sacks. Seventeen letters of love, nine of complaint, and one that just says 'ha.'
Somewhere in those sacks is a love letter that will never arrive. I like to think the river's reading it.
Neither rain nor sleet nor hippos shall keep these sacks from being slightly damp.
The mail goes through. It goes through the river, mostly. Some of it arrives.
The floating market. Forty boats, and every one is a gift shop. We needn't stop. They'll come to us.
That's the market. Everything's a bargain. That's because everything's slightly damp.
Haggle if you like. They'll go down. They'll also go up. They'll go sideways, if you let them.
Prices are fixed. They're fixed to a point somewhere near the horizon, and they move when you look.
Buy a souvenir. Nothing says 'I survived the river' like a small clay boat that doesn't float.
They sell little models of this boat. Very accurate. They leak in all the same places.
That man is selling umbrellas. On a boat. On a river. I admire the nerve and I resent the logic.
Don't make eye contact. They'll sell you a map. It's of a different river. It's better than ours.
Fog. Don't worry, I know the river. By ear. Mostly my ear, occasionally the boat's.
Lovely fog. You can't see a thing, which makes me an excellent skipper. I see no problems.
Sound the horn! If anything answers, we'll know it's a boat. If nothing does, we'll know it's also a boat.
That's the horn. It's very loud. It's so we can hear ourselves not hitting anything.
Don't worry about the shapes in the fog. Most of them are trees. The rest are also trees, but closer.
Out of the fog, a shape. It's our own reflection. We nod. We don't speak. It's tradition.
The chart says clear. The chart has never been in fog. The chart has never been anywhere.
We're navigating by dead reckoning. I'd like to stress it's the reckoning that's alive. It's the 'dead' I'm worried about.
Headroom is seven feet. The boat's eight. That's the maths. We've never got the numbers to agree.
The sign says 'Low bridge.' It's a very honest sign. It doesn't offer advice.
Three arches. The chart says four. The middle one is a rumour, and I'm taking the left.
That bridge is a hundred years old. That's older than me, in better shape, and I resent it.
Everyone down. I said down. Not 'thoughtfully down.' Down.
Heads! If you've got one, lower it. If you haven't, I'd like to meet you.
There's a toll. It's one shilling. Nobody's collected it since the war. We pay anyway, in spirit.
They say a troll lives under there. I've never seen him. I've seen the receipts.
Everything on this boat is about to rattle in a different key. Please enjoy the music.
That's washboard water. It's the river's way of giving you a free massage. Without consent.
The river's lost its temper. It'll find it again. It always does, usually downstream.
Bad day for the water. Don't take it personally. It's mostly the rocks.
Hold on to something. Not me. I'm busy. Hold something with a bit more future.
Hold the rail, and the rail holds you. It's the closest thing we have to a safety plan.
Whether you eat lunch now or later is a question the river has already answered, and the answer is 'later.'
Seasickness advice: don't look at the water. Don't look at me either. Look at the horizon, and hope.
That man's been waving since 1998. It's his job. He's very good. He's never once been thanked.
A man on a tiny island, waving. I've known him fifteen years. We've never spoken. It's the best relationship I have.
One island. One tree. One man. A complete ecosystem and a very small committee.
The island has one tree. It's the tallest on the island. It's also the shortest. It's all about perspective.
Everybody wave. He'll wave back. He always does. It's the nicest thing that happens to him all year.
Go on, wave. He does it for a living. It's only polite to give him something to do.
They say the man on the island knows the secret of the river. I asked. He waved. I took it as a yes.
Sometimes I think he's the only one who knows where the river ends. He just waves. I think that's an answer.
A cable ferry. The cable is at neck height. He is very sure it's your move.
The ferryman has right of way. He's had it forty years. We're guests.
Cable! Duck! Left! No, your other left!
That's a cable. It's taut. You'll feel a certain tension. That's the cable, and also me.
The ferryman waits for passengers. He's been waiting since the Tuesday before last. He's patient. It's his one skill.
Don't worry about the ferry. It's going nowhere. That's the whole route.
She's at full steam. That's not a warning. That's an ambition.
The gauge is in the red. It isn't alarming; it's committed.
If you hear a loud bang, that's just the boiler's way of saying it's been a pleasure.
The boiler is on fire. It's a small fire. It's proud of itself.
Everyone sit back. We're travelling at the speed of imminent.
Pressure's high. That's what I tell my doctor, too.
We're not sinking. We're descending, with dignity.
The water is at the rail. I'm told that's good for morale. It isn't. But I'm told.
If you're wondering what that sound is, it's the river coming to visit. Kindly show it the door.
There's water in the boat. Please don't think of it as 'in.' Think of it as 'we're in the water.'
It's not water. It's a new design. The 'indoor river.'
Bail, folks. It's good for the arms. And, I'm told, for the buoyancy.
She's not falling apart. She's coming undone at her own pace.
Parts of the boat are leaving. They'll send a postcard.
That wasn't a crack. That was a hello from the structure.
If any of the boat comes off in your hand, it's a souvenir. If it's the whole boat, please tell me.
Keep calm. The boat is mostly still here. It's a matter of how much 'mostly' you need.
We're held together by optimism and paint. Mostly paint. Please don't touch the paint.
Everything is under control. Not my control, but somebody's.
Don't panic. I'll do the panicking. I'm trained.
This is what we call the full experience. It's available on all bookings.
Fire above, water below. It's balanced, if you think about it. Please don't think about it.
It's all part of the show. The show is called 'Why Did We Book This.'
If anyone has questions, hold them. I haven't got answers. I've got a bucket.
